title: How do you turn facts into insights in a case interview?
description: How to move from describing numbers to explaining what they mean for the client, with a simple three-step habit and examples.
hook: You turn a fact into an insight by asking "so what?" until you reach something the client should do differently: compare the fact with something, say what it explains or rules out, then state the implication and the next thing to test. Average candidates report numbers. Strong candidates say what the numbers mean for the client, and that is a habit you can build.
body:
Fact, insight, implication

  • Fact: "Online sales grew 40%."
  • Insight: "Online is now a quarter of all sales, and it is growing much faster than stores."
  • Implication: "So the client's plan to open 20 new stores may be investing in the slower channel. I'd like to compare the return on new stores with the return on investing in online."

Most candidates stop at the fact. The marks are in the implication, and in the next test it points to.

Three questions to ask yourself

  1. Is this big or small compared with something? Last year, competitors, the market, the goal.
  2. What does it explain, or rule out? A flat price rules out price as the cause of a revenue fall.
  3. What should the client do differently because of it? If nothing, it may not matter.

A worked example

An exhibit shows that a retailer's customer visits are down 8%, average basket value is up 5%, and total sales are slightly lower. A descriptive answer repeats the three figures. A useful answer works out what they mean.

Say visits were 1M and the average basket $20, so revenue was $20M. Now visits are 920,000 and the basket is $21, so revenue is $19.32M, a 3.4% fall. The insight: fewer visits are the real problem, and higher spend per visit has only partly offset it. The implication: find out why visits fell (fewer new customers, less repeat shopping, a competitor or store closures) before doing anything else. You might end up prioritising bringing lapsed customers back rather than discounting the whole basket.

A reliable way to say it out loud is fact → insight → implication → next test. If you cannot state the implication, you may be analysing a number that does not matter to the client's goal. If you cannot propose a next test, your insight is probably too vague. See what to say when you are handed a chart for the same habit applied to exhibits.

After every calculation

Never leave a number hanging. "Break-even is 20,000 units" becomes "Break-even is 20,000 units, which is 10% of a 200,000-unit market. We already hold 15%, so it looks achievable." The calculation only earns marks once you compare it with something. More on this in getting through the maths without mistakes.

Practise it anywhere

When you read a news story about a company, ask "so what?" twice. A supermarket's prices are rising faster than inflation. So what? Shoppers might switch to discounters. So what? The supermarket may need to invest in its own-label range. A few minutes of this each day trains the reflex. The interview skills page has more short daily exercises.

1. "Our client's market share fell from 30% to 25%." Take it to an implication.

Show the answer

"Compared with what? If the market grew fast, our revenue may still be up, so I'd check the dollars first. If competitors are taking share, I'd want to know which ones and why, because the response to a cheaper rival differs from the response to a better product."

2. You calculate that a new product would add $2M of profit a year. The goal is $10M. Finish the thought.

Show the answer

"That's 20% of the $10M we need, so it helps but cannot be the whole answer. We need at least one bigger lever. I'd look at pricing next."
